examples.problem: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $2,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of $135^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
examples.worked_solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ where

$$
r=2, \quad \theta=135^{\circ}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x &= r\cos\theta\[5pt]
		 &=2 \cos\left( 135^{\circ} \right)\[5pt]
		 &= 2 \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
		 &= -\sqrt{2}
	}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		y &= r\sin\theta\[5pt]
		 &= 2 \sin\left(135^{\circ}\right)\[5pt]
		 &= 2 \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
		 &= \sqrt{2}
	}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $\left(  -\sqrt{2},  \sqrt{2}\right).$

feedback.problem:
If the point $P$ has polar coordinates $(4,\frac{7\pi }{6}),$ then its Cartesian coordinates are

$(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
feedback.worked_solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot -\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-2\sqrt{3},-2).$
